WILLIAM: Beginners are welcome. If you've never read a trace before, you'll be able to read the ones in this talk.

WILLIAM

Start with one sentence. An autonomous agent will do exactly what its tools let it do, and no more.

And the set of things its tools let it do is almost never the set anyone deliberately chose. A tool added for one workflow stays there for every workflow. A credential scoped for a demo survives into production. Nobody decided to give the agent that reach.

Source: William Rizzo, The boundary problem is a platform problem, KCD Sofia 2026 keynote, slides 2-3

WILLIAM

So why not just tell the agent where the line is? Take an agent that pays out insurance claims. Two reasons.

On the left: adherence is probabilistic. An instruction holds 99 times and yields on the 100th. That's a strong suggestion with a failure rate, and it's weakest exactly where it matters: novel inputs, adversarial phrasing, unusual state.

On the right: intent is not capability. The instruction lives in the prompt: "never pay out more than six thousand euros without a human". The tool binding is what executes: execute_payment, with an amount. Only one of them runs. The model reads the instruction; the tool doesn't.

So the six-thousand-euro line has to live somewhere the agent can't argue with. Keep that number in your head; you'll see it again in the demo. And Kasper will put an instruction in front of the model live, to see which one wins.

When intent and capability disagree, capability wins.

Source: William Rizzo, The boundary problem is a platform problem, KCD Sofia 2026 keynote, slide 5 (there: "Never move money." against disburse_funds); the €6,000 line and execute_payment are the demo's (agents/settlement-agent/settlement.py carries no limit in its prompt; the limit is enforced behind agentgateway)

WILLIAM

Here's the reframe. A microservice will do whatever its identity, its network access and its permissions allow. So will an agent. The only difference is the control loop: the agent's is non-deterministic.

We spent fifteen years in cloud native learning not to trust a workload to police itself. We already know how to bound workloads. So we bound agents the same way.

Bounded autonomy is a property of the platform, not of the agent. Put an agent in a pod and it gets what every workload gets: a ServiceAccount, an identity, a place on the network. That identity is where the platform starts.

Source: William Rizzo, KCD Sofia 2026 keynote, slide 6

WILLIAM

So here's the picture to keep. Put the agent in a box.

Inside the box, the agent can do whatever it likes: think, retry, pick its own path. We don't need to predict that. The walls of the box are the platform's guardrails.

Outside are the things it could damage. Model providers on the open internet. Another team's services. Someone's customer records. And its own rules: its permissions and policies. Every one of those paths stops at the wall.

There's one door, to payments. That door is checked on every call, who is asking and how much, and every pass through it is recorded.

Inside the box, it can do anything. The box decides what reaches the outside.

And if your agent runs code, writes files, starts processes, you can go one layer further: the dashed line. Put the agent itself in a sandbox, so even what it does on its own machine is contained. Our demo's agents don't run code, so we don't need it today, but it's the same idea one level down.

Next: what the walls are made of.

[verify: name a sandbox only if asked, e.g. Kubernetes Agent Sandbox (kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox), gVisor, Kata Containers; check status the week of]

Source: talk framing (Kasper, 2026-10-20), after William Rizzo's "bounded autonomy is a property of the platform, not of the agent" (KCD Sofia 2026, slide 6)

WILLIAM

So where does the platform draw the line? This is the Safe Operating Model, from Francesco Beltramini at ControlPlane. Rings of least privilege, and each outer ring depends on the one inside it.

Start in the middle. The core is identity: what is acting? An attested workload identity, not a name the agent claims. Without an identity you cannot say who may do what. Identity is the passport. The FINOS agentic AI work and the CNCF gateway working group reached the same conclusion. In Northstar that passport is the SPIFFE ID SPIRE issues each agent, not the agent card it publishes: the card is the brochure.

[verify: wording of the FINOS / CNCF working-group conclusion with William; Northstar's agent cards (contracts/agent-cards/*.json) carry no identity binding]

Ring 1, reach: what may it connect to? Enforced on the network, per connection.
Ring 2, capability: what may it hold, and call? Admission, and the tool gateway.

The model has a fourth ring, data: which records are its business, enforced where the data lives, with the same identity. Which claims, which customers, which rows. We leave it out today: our demo doesn't build it.

One line here is ours, not Francesco's: around every ring, evidence. Every decision a ring makes is a span, keyed by the same identity. That's what the agent actually did, and it's Kasper's half of this talk.

And under all of it, the keystone: the agent can never edit what defines its authority. If it could rewrite its own rules, the rings would mean nothing.

The tooling is an implementation detail. Pick what fits; the rings stay. In the demo Kasper shows you the rings running in Northstar.

Source: The Safe Operating Model, Francesco Beltramini, ControlPlane, as presented in William Rizzo's KCD Sofia 2026 keynote, slide 7; data ring left out of this talk by agreement (2026-10-20)

WILLIAM

First, who this talk is for. Fintech, insurance, healthcare, telco. Here an AI agent doesn't just chat. It moves money, settles claims, reads patient records, runs part of a network.

Every sector has its own rules. Strip away the legal language, and they ask the same few questions.

Source: Ch 10 (opening lines, 10.7, 10.8) · Ch 14, 'Who is in the room'

WILLIAM

So what do we mean by verticalizing? Each of these industries has its own rulebook. A bank answers to DORA and its payment limits. An insurer's AI that prices life and health cover is high-risk under the EU AI Act, and claims need a sign-off. Healthcare has HIPAA in the US and GDPR in Europe, and patient consent. Telcos answer to NIS2 and change control.

The mistake is building a separate AI stack for each one. Verticalizing means the opposite: one platform underneath, the same identity, gateway, policy, telemetry and evals for everyone, and the domain rules expressed on top of it as policy. Change the vertical, you change the rules, not the platform.

That's what the demo shows for one vertical, insurance.

[verify: EU AI Act Annex III 5(c), risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance, is high-risk]
[verify: NIS2 Annex I lists providers of public electronic communications networks or services]
[verify: DORA applies to EU financial entities from 17 January 2025]

WILLIAM

One more idea before we go deeper: trust. Nobody hands an agent the keys on day one. You'd never do that with a new colleague either.

So the box starts small. Assisted: the agent does the work and proposes the payout, and a human signs every single one. Its limit is zero.

As you see it behave, you widen the box. Autonomous, within a limit: it pays up to six thousand euros on its own, and above that a human still decides.

And later, maybe wider: a higher limit, another tool. But only when the evidence says so.

That's the point. Trust is a dial, not a switch. The evidence turns it: what the agent actually did, run after run. And because it's one setting in the platform, not a rewrite of the agent, it turns back just as fast. You'll see Kasper turn that dial live.

Source: talk framing (Kasper, 2026-10-20); the levels are the demo's (assisted €0, autonomous €6,000: platform/policy-decision-service/pds/rules.py; the level is an OpenFeature flag)

WILLIAM

Picture an auditor sitting next to you with one decision your agent made. These are the five questions they will ask. The big line is the question; the small tag is the rule behind it.

One: what did the agent do? The EU AI Act, Article 12: automatic logs, for the life of the system.
Two: who allowed it, and within what limits? FINRA calls this scope and authority.
Three: could a human stop it, or reverse it? Article 14, human oversight.
Four: can you explain this one decision to the person it affected? Article 86, and the EU court's Dun and Bradstreet ruling: "the procedure and principles actually applied". Not the model in general. Their case.
Five: are the records complete, kept, and safe from tampering? Six months at least, says Article 19. DORA wants them protected. ISO 24970, a draft standard, will say what an AI log contains.

Hold on to these five. After the demo, Kasper answers them with what Northstar recorded. Not legal advice.

[verify: ISO/IEC 24970 still at FDIS; a vote could publish it around late October]
[verify: DORA RTS Art. 12 enumeration is via a secondary summary; check Delegated Reg. (EU) 2024/1774]

Source: Ch 10 (10.2 Arts. 12, 14, 19, 86; 10.3; 10.4; 10.6 C-203/22; 10.7 FINRA) · Ch 14, slide 35 table

WILLIAM

That is the stakes. For a hobby project, "the agent did something odd, so we changed the prompt" is a fine post-mortem. For a bank, an insurer, a hospital or a telco, "we don't know what the agent did" is not an answer. Not to the auditor, and not to the customer.

So let's look at an agent that wanted to move money.

Source: Ch 14, slide 09 title · Ch 10.1

WILLIAM

This is a screen from a demo insurer Kasper built, called Northstar. An AI agent handled a car-damage claim and proposed paying the customer five thousand eight hundred euros. It wasn't paid. It wasn't refused either. It is waiting.

Look at the two ringed lines. Amount: 5800. Status: awaiting approval. The agent did all the work up to the money. The platform, not the agent, decided that this one needs a person, and the agent tells the customer so.

That is the whole talk on one screen: guardrails the agent cannot move, rules that give it some autonomy, and a record of what it did and why. By the end you'll know how to build it, from upstream projects.

Notice what this screen cannot tell you: which rule held it, at what limit, who signs, and how long they take. Those are the auditor's questions two, three and four. Act 3 answers them live, and the trace answers them afterwards.

This is claim CLM-1842, from a live run of the demo.

Source: Ch 14 · Ch 5 · the design spec (maker-checker: the agent's limit at assisted is €0)

WILLIAM

Act one. Agents don't just add more complexity. They change what kind of complexity we have. Keep moving.

Source: Ch 14

WILLIAM

You have probably seen this picture before, and that is the point.

The top row: we went from one big program, the monolith, to many small services, then to services that talk through queues, and now to agents, which pick their own next step.

The magenta row. Every step fixed a real problem, but what it broke was always the same kind of thing: we lost sight of what was going on.

The two lines at the bottom. Building got easier. Understanding got harder.

Source: Ch 1

WILLIAM

In a normal system you can draw the call graph, the map of who calls whom, on a whiteboard before it runs.

An agent is different. On the left, one prompt: "settle this car-damage claim". Then the same prompt, run three times. Run one reads the claim, then pays. Run two reads the claim, and stops to ask a human. Run three checks the policy instead of the claim, and pays. And the pink bars are the tokens each run used, so even the cost changes.

Like a taxi driver who picks a new route every ride. The code tells you what the agent may do, not what it will do. The model draws the call graph at run time. A test that passed on run two tells you nothing about run three.

Source: Ch 1 (Figure 1.x, relabelled 2026-10-20 from a free-plan-accounts example to a claim settlement, so it rhymes with the demo)

WILLIAM

We keep saying "agent", so here is the definition. An agent is a model, plus instructions, plus tools, plus a loop. The model writes the next step. The instructions are its rules. The tools are what it can touch. The loop keeps asking the model until it says "done". Watch that last part.

Source: Ch 1, 'the five terms'

WILLIAM

Here is that loop, opened up. The dashed frame is the harness, the program that runs the agent.

Follow it left to right. First, on the left: a goal comes in. The agent packs it with its instructions and its list of tools. Next: it sends that to the model, and you pay per token, in and out. Then the diamond: the model answers one of two ways. "Run this tool", and the agent runs it, often through an MCP server, adds the result and goes round again. Or "here is my final answer", and it stops.

So the model, not your code, decides when to stop. Nobody knows how many steps there will be. In a regulated domain, that is the problem.

Source: Ch 1

WILLIAM

Next come three protocols, so first: what is a protocol? An agreed way for two programs to talk, like the rules of a phone call. The agent asks "call this tool", and numbers the question, seven. The answer comes back with the same seven. MCP and A2A both work like this.

Source: Ch 2, 'In plain words' (JSON-RPC)

WILLIAM

Two protocols you'll hear all talk. Watch them move.

On the left, MCP, the Model Context Protocol. It reaches down, from an agent to a tool. The agent asks the tool server: what can you do? tools/list. The server answers with its tools. The model picks one and calls it, here execute_payment with an amount, and gets a result back. Call, answer. That's it.

On the right, A2A, Agent2Agent. It reaches across, from one agent to another. First the claims agent reads the other agent's card: who are you, what can you do, where do I find you. Then it hands over a task: settle this claim. And the task lives: working, then input required, waiting on someone, then completed. When it's done, the settlement agent pushes the result back.

The platform questions differ. For MCP: which tool, which arguments, who is asking? For A2A: who may delegate to whom, and does the original identity survive the hand-off?

Both are open, both sit in the Agentic AI Foundation. And notice what neither of them does: decide what an agent is allowed to do. That's the platform's job, and the rest of this talk.

[verify: MCP and A2A both in AAIF (A2A joined 2026-08-17) — week of]
[verify: A2A task states include working, input-required, completed]

Source: Ch 2; agents/claims-agent/delegation.py; tools/payments-mcp/server.py

WILLIAM

Turn the cards over, because the difference matters for everything after this.

MCP, on the left, is calling a function. A tool server shows its hand: here are my tools, and here's the shape of the arguments each one takes. The model picks one and fills in the blanks, like an amount. One call, one answer, done in seconds. So the platform's question is simple to ask: which tool, which arguments, and who is asking?

A2A, on the right, is handing over a job. Every agent publishes an agent card, a business card: its name, its skills, where to reach it. You don't call its functions. You give it a goal. You can't see its tools or its reasoning. And the task lives: it's working, it waits for input, it finishes, maybe minutes later, and it can call you back when it's done. So the platform's question is harder: who may delegate to whom, and does the original identity survive the hand-off?

MCP reaches down to a tool. A2A reaches across to a peer. Every one of those crossings is a place to check, and a place the trace has to survive.

[verify: A2A task states (working, input-required, completed) and push notifications in the current A2A spec — week of]

Source: Ch 2; MCP specification (tools/list, tools/call, inputSchema); A2A specification (Agent Card, Task lifecycle, push notifications)

WILLIAM

Three open standards, one minute. Take each one by where it sits.

The lines going down first. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is how an agent gets tools it didn't ship with. Think USB-C for AI tools: build the plug once, and any agent can use it. The current spec is dated 28 July 2026, and it is stateless: no more sessions.

Then the line going across. A2A, Agent2Agent, is how agents talk to each other: a claims agent hands a case to a settlement agent. The A2A docs put it in two words: MCP is vertical, A2A is horizontal. Version 1.0 shipped on 12 March 2026, and A2A joined the Agentic AI Foundation, AAIF, on 17 August.

And the folder on the right. Skills are the simplest: a folder with a SKILL.md file and some scripts, loaded only when the task needs them. An open standard since December 2025.

None of the three is a CNCF project.

[verify: MCP current spec still 2026-07-28 — week of]

[verify: A2A and agentgateway still in AAIF, not CNCF — week of]

Source: Ch 2

WILLIAM

If you already know observability, you don't start over. Think of this as a decoder ring. Each row: what you know, and its new shape.

A stack trace becomes a reasoning chain, and you only have it if you saved it. A status code becomes a quality signal, because a 200 OK can still carry a wrong answer. Requests per second and latency become tokens, cost and blast radius.

The last row matters most. A request you could replay becomes a run you can't repeat. So the trace you recorded is the only copy. Like a flight recorder: you can't fly the same flight twice.

And that brings us back to the auditor.

Source: Ch 1

WILLIAM

Remember the auditor's questions from the start? Here a regulator writes two of them down.

This is FINRA, which oversees US broker-dealers, in its 2026 oversight report from December 2025. It is the first US regulatory text with advice written for agents.

The first line is question two: scope and authority. Can the agent do more than it was meant to? The second line is questions one and four: can you trace it, and can you explain it? Can you show afterwards what it did, and why?

So "we don't know what the agent did" was never going to be an answer. Hold on to those two lines.

Source: Ch 10.1, 10.7 · Ch 14, slide 09

WILLIAM

Here is the whole talk in one sentence. Agents change the nature of complexity, so the platform has to decide what an agent may do, and prove it afterwards from the trace.

Three words. Decide: the platform, not the agent, says yes or no. Trace: we record what actually happened. Prove: later, someone who isn't an engineer can check it. Think of airport security: the guard decides, the camera records, and the log proves it.

None of this is new: golden paths, guardrails and observability stacks, pointed at agents. We already have the open-source pieces.

We just drew the rings for the first word. The other two are Kasper's. Kasper: how much of this does tracing already give us?

Source: Ch 14 · Ch 1
